lessons.title: Leaf Structure: The Architecture of a Photosynthetic Machine

quiz.prompt: A pair of Grade 10 students in Kisumu examines a bean leaf cross-section under a microscope. Where on the leaf should they look to find the most stomata with their pairs of guard cells?
choices: The upper epidermis
Inside the vascular bundle
The palisade mesophyll
The lower epidermis
quiz.rationale: Stomata are pores found mainly in the lower epidermis, each surrounded by two guard cells. The teacher directs students to scan the lower epidermis when they cannot find stomata.
quiz.placement: Observe Step 4: locate stomata on the lower epidermis and sketch a single stoma with its two guard cells

quiz.prompt: In a cross-section of a mango leaf, one layer lies just below the upper epidermis. It is made of tall cells packed closely together in a row. What is this layer called?
choices: Lower epidermis
Palisade mesophyll
Spongy mesophyll
Phloem
quiz.rationale: The palisade mesophyll sits directly beneath the upper epidermis and is made of densely packed, column-shaped cells. Spongy mesophyll lies below it and has loosely arranged cells with air spaces.
quiz.placement: Observe Step 3: shade and label every distinct layer on the printed outline diagram

quiz.prompt: The cuticle and upper epidermis form the top surface of a leaf. How does their structure help the leaf make food?
choices: They have many large air spaces for storing carbon dioxide
They carry sugars away from the leaf to the rest of the plant
They are transparent, so light can pass through to the cells below
They are full of chloroplasts, so they absorb most of the light
quiz.rationale: The cuticle and epidermis are transparent, which lets light pass through to the palisade cells underneath. They do not carry out most light capture, store gases or transport sugars.
quiz.placement: Explain: jigsaw expert group presentations (epidermis/cuticle group)

quiz.prompt: Why are the palisade mesophyll cells tightly packed and found near the top of the leaf?
choices: So that they can carry water up from the roots
So that their chloroplasts get as much light as possible
So that water vapour can escape easily from the leaf
So that carbon dioxide can move freely through large gaps between them
quiz.rationale: Being near the upper surface and densely packed gives the palisade cells the most exposure of chloroplasts to light. Large gaps for gas movement belong to the spongy mesophyll, and water transport is the job of the xylem.
quiz.placement: Explain: jigsaw expert group presentations (palisade mesophyll group)

quiz.prompt: The spongy mesophyll of a leaf has many air spaces between its cells. What is the main function of these air spaces?
choices: They store water for the plant to use when it is hot
They carry sugars made in the leaf to the roots
They reflect light back up to the palisade cells
They allow carbon dioxide to diffuse to the cells inside the leaf
quiz.rationale: The air spaces in the spongy mesophyll let carbon dioxide that enters through the stomata diffuse to the cells inside the leaf. Sugars are carried by the phloem, and water is supplied by the xylem.
quiz.placement: Explain: jigsaw expert group presentations (spongy mesophyll/air spaces group)

quiz.prompt: A vascular bundle in a leaf contains xylem and phloem. Which statement correctly describes what they do?
choices: Xylem and phloem both let carbon dioxide into the leaf
Phloem brings water and minerals into the leaf; xylem carries sugars out of the leaf
Xylem opens and closes the stomata; phloem absorbs light
Xylem brings water and minerals into the leaf; phloem carries sugars out of the leaf
quiz.rationale: The xylem supplies water and minerals to the leaf, while the phloem exports the sugars the leaf makes. Mixing up the two tissues is a common error.
quiz.placement: Explain: jigsaw expert group presentations (vascular bundles group)

quiz.prompt: Open stomata let carbon dioxide into the leaf and oxygen out. What else leaves the leaf through open stomata?
choices: Chlorophyll
Minerals from the soil
Water vapour
Sugars
quiz.rationale: Water vapour also escapes through open stomata, which is the key to explaining midday wilting. Sugars and minerals move in the phloem and xylem, not out through stomata.
quiz.placement: Explain: synthesis question 'What else moves through an open stoma besides gases?'

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki plants in a Nairobi kitchen garden wilt at midday in strong sun, even though the soil is still moist. Which explanation best uses leaf structure to explain this?
choices: The soil has run out of water by midday, so the roots cannot take any in
The hot sun burns and kills the palisade cells, so the leaves fall over
Stomata are wide open, so water vapour is lost faster than the xylem can supply water, and the cells lose turgor
The phloem stops carrying sugars at midday, so the leaves have no food and droop
quiz.rationale: At midday the stomata open wide and water vapour escapes faster than the xylem can replace it, so cells lose turgor and the leaves wilt. The damage is not permanent, because the plants recover overnight, and the soil is still moist.
quiz.placement: Model: revise the Lesson 1 model with arrows for water up the xylem and water vapour out of the stoma

quiz.prompt: Sukuma wiki plants moved under the shade of a mango tree stop wilting, but over several weeks their leaves turn pale yellowish-green and they grow more slowly. Which explanation best fits what the class learnt about leaf structure?
choices: The mango tree roots take all the carbon dioxide from the soil
The shade makes the stomata lose water faster, so the leaves dry out
Less light reaches the palisade cells, so the leaves capture less light to make food
The shade blocks the xylem, so no water reaches the leaves
quiz.rationale: In shade, less light reaches the palisade mesophyll, so the leaf's light-capturing ability drops, which leads to paleness and slow growth. Shade actually reduces wilting, so faster water loss is not the cause.
quiz.placement: After the whole lesson (revisiting the sukuma wiki phenomenon)
